rows.Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale
rows.Risk Statement: As AI is adopted at scale and used for higher consequence decisions, technology continues to evolve more rapidly than regulators can respond. Managing risks around the identification and protection of unique proprietary data will become a decisive source of competitive advantage.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Movement beyond using AI for productivity and into evidence generation, regulatory content and clinical development. 
• Adoption may outpace regulations which remain immature and globally inconsistent. 
• Competitive advantage shifting toward organisations that can mobilise unique data at scale.
rows.Action Detail: Build validation and approved-use architecture before AI-supported outputs are embedded in regulated decisions at scale. Establish where AI outputs require human-in-the-loop assurance versus where autonomous operation is a conscious and tolerable choice. Prioritise provenance standards, proprietary data as a strategic asset, and protection against shadow AI in sensitive processes.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Potential to compromise defensibility of regulatory submissions, clinical decisions, and commercial content with reputational exposure. 
• Limiting of ability to build competitive advantage from proprietary data.
rows.Key Active Triggers: AI-supported outputs in regulated submissions without validated assurance; repeated data-provenance concerns in high-consequence workflows; shadow AI in sensitive processes; jurisdictional restrictions constraining AI use in key markets; inability to mobilise proprietary data for competitive purposes within acceptable timeframes.
rows.Related SET Areas: R&D; Medical; Commercial; IT; Regulatory; Quality; Manufacturing; Clinical; Compliance

rows.Risk Statement: Risk of critical dependencies on a small number of externally controlled cloud, compute, and software ecosystems with potential exposures to restrictions in the availability of systems that cannot easily be replaced.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Access to AI models, compute and platforms is an emerging strategic and geopolitical issue. 
• Access may be restricted or withdrawn for reasons outside AZ's control.
• Concentration has deepened during rapid AI adoption.
rows.Action Detail: Establish AZ's position on acceptable concentration in critical digital ecosystems. Determine where single-provider dependency requires diversification or contingency — and where current dependency is a conscious and tolerable choice given switching costs. Prioritise cloud, AI-model, and enterprise-software decisions where switching costs are highest and restriction risk most credible.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Disruption to critical capabilities that are vital to strategy potentially forcing duplication. 
• Externally imposed constraints on capabilities that underpin innovation at speed and operational efficiency.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Material dependence on fewer than three providers for any critical digital capability; model withdrawal or feature restriction in any jurisdiction; sovereignty rules requiring infrastructure current architecture cannot accommodate; licensing changes materially altering cost or use rights; major outage with no validated alternative pathway.
rows.Related SET Areas: IT / Digital; Cyber; R&D; Operations; Procurement; Finance; Enterprise Risk

rows.Risk Statement: A shift to advanced, automated manufacturing may outpace supply chain resilience and capabilities increasing the risk of supply disruption, delayed launches or compliance issues.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Accelerating adoption of advanced manufacturing with embedded AI.
• Certain supply chains, infrastructure, and regulations maturing more slowly.
• New dependencies and vulnerabilities may become visible and more material as pace increases.
rows.Action Detail: Build future-state resilience into manufacturing investment decisions before fragility compounds. Establish acceptable single-point-of-failure exposure for launch-critical and high-revenue supply chains — and where the cost of redundancy is justified versus where concentrated risk is a conscious choice. Prioritise N-tier visibility, cyber-physical resilience, and long-term site-portfolio fit.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Supply disruption, delayed launches, quality or compliance issues. 
• Specifically, new modalities require investment, navigation of qualification criteria and narrower supplier options.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Single qualified site or supplier for any launch-critical or top-20 revenue product; repeated validation bottlenecks delaying release; cyber-physical incident affecting quality or safety systems; inability to map dependencies below Tier 2 for priority supply chains; sustained underutilisation or strategic mismatch in material parts of the network.
rows.Related SET Areas: Operations; Manufacturing; Supply Chain; Quality; Engineering; External Manufacturing; Procurement; IT / Digital

rows.Risk Statement: Rapid digital adoption, advances in science and technology and increased competition for critical talent may outpace the ability to attract, develop, and retain the workforce and specialist capabilities needed.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Upcoming workforce transition driven by AI, requiring the organisation and monitoring of agents alongside humans (to varying degrees depending on the part of the business / roles)
• Demand for new, specialist or scarce skills rising faster than many organisations can reskill or hire at scale.
rows.Action Detail: Identify where capability erosion could materially undermine strategic execution over a 5-10 year horizon. Establish which roles and developmental pathways are strategically non-negotiable versus where automation or external sourcing is an acceptable long-term model. Prioritise specialist succession depth, change-absorption capacity, and acceptable dependence on scarce external talent.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Reduced capacity to deliver strategy, slower innovation, and weaker succession pipelines.
• Higher external dependencies.
• Critical single points of failure could reduce the capacity to deliver change.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Inability to fill critical roles within acceptable timeframes; growing dependence on single individuals without validated succession; reduction in internal developmental pathways to senior expert roles; rising attrition or burnout in strategically critical populations; increasing vendor dependence for capabilities previously held in-house.
rows.Related SET Areas: HR; R&D; Operations; Finance; IT / Digital; Quality; Regulatory; Commercial

rows.Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition
rows.Risk Statement: Advances in science and technology may outpace the ability to adapt. New breakthroughs or unexpected competitors could make science, pipeline, or products less relevant before loss of exclusivity, reducing competitiveness.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Scientific and technological change accelerating, while competitors and new entrants may move faster to apply it, compressing timelines. 
• AI-first companies could scale in AZ relevant therapy areas and novel assets may face competition sooner. 
• China-origin innovation rapidly reaching global quality.
rows.Action Detail: Reposition portfolio, partnering, and development-model choices before relevance windows compress further. Establish where AZ needs to accelerate development speed, build platform capability, or act early on BD — versus where current competitive assumptions remain sound. Focus on therapy areas where mechanism crowding or AI-native competitors create the greatest risk of earlier-than-assumed relevance loss.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Potential for earlier revenue erosion and reduced pipeline value. 
• Risks of loss of competitive position and higher execution risk given the potential need to rapidly adapt.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Competitors achieving materially faster development timelines in AZ's priority areas; AI-first entrants scaling clinical programmes in adjacent spaces; greater-than-expected mechanism-class crowding around AZ pipeline assets; peer data demonstrating equivalent efficacy in AZ's priority indications; alliance structures creating decision-speed penalties versus single-entity competitors.
rows.Related SET Areas: R&D; Strategy; Business Development; Commercial; Medical; Market Access; Finance

rows.Risk Statement: Rising geopolitical tension and increasing legal and regulatory divergence may create a more fragmented operating environment, disrupting supply and reducing strategic flexibility.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Governments are placing greater emphasis on regulatory sovereignty. 
• Increasing likelihood of trade restrictions, export controls, sanctions and divergent legal requirements.
rows.Action Detail: Identify which elements of AZ's global operating model face credible viability risk from legal conflict, export restriction, or sovereignty requirements — and where the cost of regional redesign is justified versus where AZ accepts residual exposure to fragmentation. Prioritise cross-border data flows, China-related exposure, supply-chain localisation, and areas where conflicting requirements may become irreconcilable.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Higher operating and compliance costs and the potential to progressively constrain where AZ can innovate, partner, manufacture and move data. 
• Reduced ability to operate as one integrated, global enterprise. 
• In acute scenarios, could require choices between jurisdictions accepting non-compliance in one to maintain it in another.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Export controls restricting tools, data, or collaboration relevant to AZ; industrial policy changing sourcing or capital economics in key markets; legal requirements in one jurisdiction creating direct conflict with another; sanctions affecting partners, suppliers, or markets; mandatory localisation of supply chains or data; material acceleration in China-origin competitive capability relevant to AZ's portfolio.
rows.Related SET Areas: Strategy; Government Affairs; Legal; R&D; Operations; Finance; Procurement; IT / Digital; Compliance

rows.Risk Statement: Rising pressure on healthcare costs and public budgets may impact on the ability to sustain pricing, reimbursement, and patient access. Constrained uptake of innovative medicines and weakening in the funding available to support future R&D.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Healthcare systems facing growing pressure from ageing populations, higher disease burden and inflation. 
• Payers increasing scrutiny of medicine prices, comparative value and speed of access. 
• Expectations include representativeness, equity, and affordability.
rows.Action Detail: Influence the value and policy environment before structural funding pressure hardens into irreversible constraints. Establish where AZ needs to lead on affordability or evidence-strategy innovation versus where current approaches remain adequate. Prioritise markets where launch economics are most sensitive to payer pushback, intermediary control is growing fastest, and AI-enabled price benchmarking may accelerate transparency.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Pricing and margin pressure. 
• Slower or more restricted reimbursement and access leading to a reduced return on innovation.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Payer or policy decisions changing launch-pricing assumptions for near-term pipeline assets; fiscal measures in major markets targeting innovative medicine budgets; intermediaries or AI tools exerting greater control over formulary positioning; evidence challenged on representativeness or equity in ways affecting access; cross-market transparency mechanisms creating material reference-pricing pressure.
rows.Related SET Areas: Market Access; Commercial; Medical; Corporate Affairs; HEOR; Regulatory; Legal; Finance

• Payers increasing scrutiny of medicine prices, comparative value and speed of access. 
• Expectations include representativeness, equity, and affordability.
rows.Action Detail: Influence the value and policy environment before structural funding pressure hardens into irreversible constraints. Establish where AZ needs to lead on affordability or evidence-strategy innovation versus where current approaches remain adequate. Prioritise markets where launch economics are most sensitive to payer pushback, intermediary control is growing fastest, and AI-enabled price benchmarking may accelerate transparency.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Pricing and margin pressure. 
• Slower or more restricted reimbursement and access leading to a reduced return on innovation.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Payer or policy decisions changing launch-pricing assumptions for near-term pipeline assets; fiscal measures in major markets targeting innovative medicine budgets; intermediaries or AI tools exerting greater control over formulary positioning; evidence challenged on representativeness or equity in ways affecting access; cross-market transparency mechanisms creating material reference-pricing pressure.
rows.Related SET Areas: Market Access; Commercial; Medical; Corporate Affairs; HEOR; Regulatory; Legal; Finance

rows.Cluster: Sustainability, resilience and pressures on health systems
rows.Risk Statement: Environmental, and broader system pressures may outpace the resilience of healthcare systems. Climate stress, environmental regulation, resource constraints and other health system pressures may make current products, sites, and sourcing models less sustainable.
rows.Why Emerging:
• Climate resilience, environmental stress and resource constraints placing greater strain on healthcare systems.
• Increasing pressure to adapt while operating in a more volatile external environment.
rows.Action Detail: Build sustainability resilience into footprint, sourcing, and product-design decisions before external standards or physical stress reduce options. Establish where current operating assumptions face credible viability risk — and where proactive investment now avoids materially higher remediation cost later. Prioritise critical-input security, water and permit risk at key sites, emerging chemical requirements, and nature-related disclosure obligations.
rows.Potential Enterprise Impact:
• Supply and operating disruption. 
• Potential revenue, reputational and patient supply impacts.
rows.Key Active Triggers: Mandatory scope 3 or nature-related standards requiring capital or reformulation investment not in plan; strategic inputs becoming volatile or subject to sourcing restrictions; water, weather, or permit constraints affecting any top-10 manufacturing site; regulatory review of chemicals in current AZ products; sustainability-linked procurement criteria materially affecting tender competitiveness.
rows.Related SET Areas: Sustainability; Operations; Manufacturing; Procurement; Market Access; Finance; Government Affairs; R&D
